# Source estimation {#sec-source-estimation}

Three parts of Alakazam estimate cortical sources: the source projections of
the 3D brain view (@sec-tr-brain3d), the Source Estimate step that stores an
estimate on a node (@sec-tr-sourceestimate), and the source cluster test
(@sec-source-cluster). They share one forward model and one inverse, and this
chapter describes both, and above all what their result can and cannot mean.

## The forward model

Alakazam uses template anatomy throughout: FieldTrip's template boundary
element head model, template 10-5 electrode positions matched by channel
label, and a template cortical sheet of 20 484, 8 196 or 5 124 vertices
[@oostenveld2011]. No individual MRI and no digitised electrode positions are
used, and there is no co-registration. Channels whose label the 10-5 system
does not know are dropped rather than placed by guesswork. The leadfield is
built on first use and cached per channel set and source space.

Template anatomy and template electrode positions are a known and
substantial source of localisation error [@akalinacar2013]. They make every
subject's estimate comparable on one sheet, which is what a group test needs,
at the price of placing no subject's sources exactly.

## The inverse

The inverse is a **distributed** solution [@hamalainen1994]: one dipole at
every vertex of the sheet, its orientation fixed to the local cortical
normal or left free and reduced to a magnitude, and only its amplitude
estimated. It is not dipole fitting, in which the number, position and
orientation of a few generators are themselves estimated [@michel2019];
that is Dipole Fit (@sec-tr-dipolefit), on the same head model.

| Method | What it is | Offered in |
|-------|-------------------------------------------------------|---------------------------------------------|
| **dSPM** | Minimum norm, with each vertex divided by its own noise standard deviation [@dale2000] | 3D view, Source Estimate, source cluster test |
| **sLORETA** | Minimum norm standardised by its resolution matrix [@pascualmarqui2002] | 3D view, Source Estimate, source cluster test |
| **eLORETA** | Exact low-resolution tomography, zero localisation error for a single source, not noise-normalised [@pascualmarqui2007] | 3D view only |

: The inverse methods. {#tbl-inverse-methods}

FieldTrip computes the spatial filter; Alakazam projects the data through it
and applies the method's scaling and the orientation along one shared path,
which keeps the dSPM normalisation explicit. An independent implementation
is kept as a reference, and the two agree to floating-point precision on the
test data.

### The noise covariance {#sec-noise-covariance}

dSPM divides each vertex by the noise it would show if the data were noise
alone, so it needs to know what the noise is. Average records it: the
covariance of the samples up to the event, pooled over every trial, by
FieldTrip's own definition (`ft_timelockanalysis` with
`cfg.covariance = 'yes'`), and divided for each bin by the number of trials
that bin's average holds, since an average of *N* trials carries a *N*th of
a single trial's noise. A trial with a rejected sample in the baseline is
left out of the estimate.

With that covariance, dSPM is FieldTrip's minimum norm as its tutorial sets
it up for an ERP: the leadfield prewhitened by the noise covariance, the
source covariance scaled to it, and the regularisation set by a
signal-to-noise ratio, λ = 1/SNR², with SNR = 3 by default, MNE's
convention [@dale2000]. A value then reads as standard deviations of the
baseline noise. Every bin of a dataset is inverted through the same spatial
filter, so conditions are compared through one operator; a bin averaged
from fewer trials has more noise, and its dSPM values are lower by the
square root of the ratio.

Without a baseline covariance (a dataset averaged before Alakazam stored
one, epochs that start at the event, or a grand average) the noise is taken
as white: equal and independent on every channel, a scaled identity, with
the regularisation set as a fraction of the leadfield's power. **Noise
covariance** in Source Estimate chooses between the two, and the 3D view
and the source cluster test use the baseline whenever every dataset
involved has one. The cluster test never mixes the two: one subject without
a covariance makes it white noise for everyone, and the report says which
was used. sLORETA and eLORETA are FieldTrip's, which work from the data's
own covariance, so the noise covariance does not change them.

A step after Average that mixes the channels (Interpolate, Collapse
Hemispheres) drops the covariance, since the noise of the mixed channels is
no longer the one it describes; a step that only removes channels keeps the
rest of it. A filter applied to an average after averaging is not reflected
in it. The regularisation is reported both as the setting and as the value
the solver used.

## Beamformers {#sec-beamformers}

A beamformer is a different kind of inverse: instead of one solution for
every vertex at once, it builds an adaptive spatial filter for each location
from the data's own covariance, passing activity from there and suppressing
it from everywhere else [@vanveen1997]. It needs single trials, since the
filter is made from their variability, and it answers a different question:
not what the ERP looks like at each vertex, but where power changes between
two windows. LCMV [@vanveen1997] does so in the time domain; DICS
[@gross2001] does so at one frequency, from the cross-spectral density,
which suits an induced oscillation that averages out of an ERP.

Beamformer (@sec-tr-beamformer) follows FieldTrip's recipe for such a
contrast. The covariance (or the cross-spectra, by multitaper) is estimated
in both windows by `ft_timelockanalysis` (or `ft_freqanalysis`); one filter
is made from both windows of every chosen bin together, so that a difference
between windows or bins is a difference in the data rather than in the
filters; and each bin's power in each window is passed through it by
`ft_sourceanalysis`. The windows must be equally long, since a covariance
from more samples is a different estimate for that reason alone.
Correlated sources, such as the two auditory cortices responding together,
are a beamformer's known weakness: the filter suppresses one with the other.

### A volume grid

The other source estimates use the template cortical sheet. A beamformer is
as often computed on a regular grid of points inside the brain
(`ft_prepare_sourcemodel`, 10 mm apart by default), which also reaches deep
structures the sheet does not cover. Its map is drawn by interpolating it
onto FieldTrip's template MRI (`ft_sourceinterpolate`) and cutting three
slices through its peak; the left hemisphere is on the left.

## What the estimate is, and is not

**It does not locate sources.** The source positions are fixed before any
data are seen; only an amplitude per vertex is estimated.

**It is not unique.** With many more vertices than electrodes, infinitely
many source distributions reproduce the scalp data exactly
[@baillet2001; @grech2008]. Minimum-norm estimation picks the one with the
smallest total power. That choice is a prior, not a property of the data, and
a different prior gives a different estimate that fits equally well.

**It carries no more patterns than there are channels.** The number of
distinguishable spatial patterns is bounded by the channel count, not by the
vertex count. For a 29-channel recording, the leadfield with orientations on
the cortical normal has rank 28 after average referencing, and 90% of its
energy lies in 6 components. The vertex count decides how smooth the map
looks, not how much it says, which is why a coarser sheet changes the run
time far more than the result: a whole-epoch estimate left 5.62% of the
scalp data unexplained on the 5 124-vertex sheet and 5.58% on the 20 484-vertex
sheet.

**Its values are not currents.** dSPM divides by a noise standard deviation
and sLORETA by an estimated source variance; both give a noise-normalised
statistic. The group test then replaces that with a *t* statistic across
subjects. A source cluster map is two transformations away from any physical
quantity. The three methods' scales are not comparable with each other, nor
with the scalp maps' microvolts, and each map carries its own label.

**Its resolution is limited by point spread.** Every vertex's estimate is a
weighted mixture of activity over a surrounding region, described by the
point-spread and cross-talk functions of the resolution matrix
[@hauk2011; @hauk2022]. Measured on a 29-channel montage and the 5 124-vertex
sheet, the spatial dispersion runs from about 34 to 63 mm depending on where
a vertex sits, and dSPM's peak is displaced by a median of about 41 mm.
eLORETA places a single source exactly, as its definition requires, and
spreads just as widely: displacement and spread are separate limits, and a
method can avoid one without avoiding the other. The source cluster report
draws the point spread of its strongest cluster's peak vertex for this
reason.

**What a result supports.** A significant source cluster supports the
statement that the conditions differ, and that the model attributes the
difference to approximately this region of a template cortex. It does not
establish a focal generator at the reported coordinate. The peak MNI
coordinate is given beside the atlas region so that the distinction stays
visible.

## Orientation

A free-orientation estimate gives three dipole components per vertex,
reduced by default to their length, which is always positive and so cannot
show polarity. **Signed (cortical normal)** takes the component along the
normal instead, keeping the sign. Pyramidal cells lie perpendicular to the
cortical sheet, which makes the normal the usual orientation constraint for
EEG, and in a group test a signed estimate has a meaningful null where a
magnitude would make the whole cortex differ from zero.

## Storing estimates

Source Estimate (@sec-tr-sourceestimate) stores an estimate on a node, and
the 3D view and the source cluster test use it instead of inverting again,
but only after two checks:

| Check | What it catches |
|----------------|-------------------------------------------------------|
| Settings | An estimate made with different channels, mesh, method, orientation, regularisation, noise covariance, time window or rate: a different answer, not a different precision. |
| Data fingerprint | The settings match but the data do not. Every step below Source Estimate copies the stored estimate forward, so a Baseline after it would otherwise carry an estimate of its parent's data. |

: The checks before a stored estimate is reused. {#tbl-source-reuse}

On a mismatch the estimate is computed again, and the report says how many
subjects were reused. The channel set is part of the key, so estimates are
reused across a study only when every subject has the same montage, which is
worth arranging for the analysis itself in any case. A whole-epoch estimate
at full rate takes about 500 MB per subject on the 20 484-vertex sheet and
130 MB on the 5 124-vertex one; the dialog shows the size before computing.
